transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… thank you for seeing me. I’m not usually someone who needs help with this sort of thing—I’ve always been the one with the lists and the plan, you know? But since my wife’s fall, I just… I’m not managing very well.

I’ll sit at the kitchen table staring at her medication chart and either start crying or get sharp over something tiny, which I’m not proud of. And things are piling up—bills, mentoring calls I should return, even basic housework. I keep telling myself I’ll get on top of it, but I just can’t seem to make myself function the way I normally do. Is that… the kind of thing you mean?
How long have you been feeling this way?
About two months, I suppose… since my wife had her fall and everything at home changed. I kept thinking it was just an adjustment period and I’d settle down, but it’s been going on since then.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things that usually bring you pleasure, like hobbies or spending time with loved ones?

I’m not sure I’d say I don’t enjoy them exactly… I mean, I haven’t really been doing much for pleasure lately. There’s been so much to keep track of that I suppose I haven’t stopped to notice.

When I’m with family, I’m glad they’re there, truly. It’s just… I may not feel quite as light or interested as I normally would. But I don’t want to overstate it. Does that make sense?
Have you found that things you usually enjoy, like hobbies or time with family, don’t bring you the same pleasure or satisfaction as they used to?

I honestly don’t know that I can answer that properly. I haven’t really been doing my usual hobbies enough to judge, and family time is… well, I’m grateful for it. It’s not as carefree as it used to be, maybe, but I wouldn’t want to say it brings me no pleasure.

Maybe I’m just a bit too preoccupied to notice. Is that the sort of thing you’re trying to get at?
When you do have time with family or engage in activities you used to enjoy, do you find that you’re not really getting the same satisfaction or pleasure out of them anymore?

I’m… not sure I can say that, no. I mean, when I’m with my family I still value it, and I’m glad to see them. It may not feel quite as easy or satisfying as before, but I don’t know if that’s because I’m not enjoying it or because my mind is elsewhere.

I don’t want to give you the wrong impression. I haven’t really tested it, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, since your wife’s fall?

Most of the day… I suppose, yes, more than I’d like to admit. Since my wife’s fall, I’ve not really felt like myself.

I used to be the one with the lists and the plan, you know, keeping everything moving. And now I’ll sit at the kitchen table staring at her medication chart and just… cry, or get sharp with someone over nothing. I’m embarrassed saying that.

It’s not that I’m trying to fall apart, but bills and mentoring calls and even basic housework have started piling up, and I just can’t seem to make myself function the way I normally would. Is that the sort of thing you mean?
Have you noticed a loss of interest in activities you used to care about, like your hobbies or responsibilities, since your wife’s fall?

I don’t think I’d put it as a clear “loss of interest,” exactly. I mean… I’m not doing as much, but I’m not sure that’s because I don’t care about those things anymore.

The hobbies and responsibilities still matter to me. I just haven’t really had the same space for them, if that makes sense. I don’t want to overstate it or make it sound worse than it is.
Can you recall a recent time when you felt genuinely happy or satisfied doing something you used to enjoy?

I’m trying to think of one… I don’t want to say “no” too quickly, because that sounds rather bleak, doesn’t it?

There have been moments where I’ve been glad to be doing something familiar, or relieved to have a bit of normality. But genuinely happy or satisfied… I’m not sure I can point to a clear example recently. Maybe I just haven’t been paying attention properly.
Would you say that you feel down, sad, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, since your wife’s fall?

Yes… I think I’d have to say yes, though I don’t like admitting that.

Since my wife’s fall, I’ve gone from being the one with the lists and the plan to sitting at the kitchen table staring at her medication chart and crying, or snapping over nothing. And things I’d normally keep on top of — bills, mentoring calls, even basic housework — they’re piling up.

I’m trying not to make too much of it, but it does feel like I just can’t make myself function the way I usually would. Is that… is that what you’re asking?
Would you say you've lost interest in things you used to care about, like your hobbies or responsibilities, since your wife's fall?

I’m not sure I’d say I’ve lost interest, exactly. It’s more that I haven’t had the energy or room in my head for those things lately.

I still care about them — I don’t want you to think I’ve just stopped caring. But I suppose, yes, they’ve slipped into the background since her fall. I’m not sure if that counts as losing interest, or just being overwhelmed.
Would you say that you’ve stopped engaging in activities you used to care about, not just because you’re overwhelmed, but because you no longer find them meaningful or worth doing?

I don’t think I’d put it quite that strongly, no.

It’s not that they feel meaningless, or that I’ve decided they’re not worth doing anymore. I think… I still believe they matter. I just don’t seem to get to them, or I can’t quite summon whatever it takes to start.

Maybe that sounds like I’m splitting hairs. I’m just trying to answer you properly. It feels more like I’ve been knocked off course than that I’ve stopped caring.
Would you say that activities you used to enjoy, like your hobbies or time with family, feel less pleasurable or satisfying to you now compared to before your wife’s fall?

I’m… not sure I can answer that cleanly.

I haven’t really tested it, if that makes sense. I’m not doing much of those things lately, so I don’t know whether they’d feel less pleasurable or whether I’m just too preoccupied to notice. When I’m with family, I’m glad they’re there, but I suppose I’m not fully present the way I used to be.

I don’t want to overstate it. It’s more that everything feels a bit muted right now, but I couldn’t honestly say I’ve stopped enjoying things altogether. Is that a fair way to put it?
Looking back, would you say that activities you used to enjoy, like your hobbies or spending time with family, have become noticeably less enjoyable or satisfying since your wife’s fall?

I’m sorry, I’m probably not giving you a very clear answer.

I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed a definite drop in enjoyment, exactly. It’s more that I’m not really doing those things in the same way, so it’s hard to compare. When I do spend time with family, I’m glad to see them, I do appreciate it… but I may not be taking it in the way I used to.

So, noticeably less satisfying? Maybe a little, but I’m not sure I’d want to call it that. It might just be that my mind is elsewhere. Does that make sense?
Would you say that, even when you do engage in activities you used to enjoy, you don’t get much pleasure or satisfaction from them anymore?

I don’t think I can honestly say that, no.

When I do manage to do something I used to enjoy, there is still some pleasure in it. Maybe it doesn’t land as fully as it used to, or I’m distracted, but it’s not as if there’s nothing there. I wouldn’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

So… I suppose the answer is, not really. It may be dulled a bit, but I can still get something from it. Is that the distinction you’re asking about?
Would you say that, in the past two months, you’ve gotten significantly less pleasure or satisfaction out of things you used to enjoy, even when you’re not distracted or preoccupied?

I don’t think I could say “significantly,” no. At least, not in a clear way.

If I’m genuinely not distracted or preoccupied, I think I can still enjoy things. Maybe not quite with the same ease as before, but there’s still something there. I wouldn’t want to exaggerate it and say I get no satisfaction from things anymore.

So… I suppose my answer would be that I haven’t really noticed that, not in a definite way. Is that helpful?
Would you say that your mood has been consistently low or sad most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at a time since your wife’s fall?

I… yes, I think so. I don’t want to overstate it, but since her fall I haven’t really felt like myself.

I used to be the one with the lists and the plan, you know, keeping things moving. Lately I can end up sitting at the kitchen table just staring at her medication chart, and I’ll cry, or I’ll snap over something that really doesn’t deserve it. It’s not every single minute, but it has felt like this heaviness is there most days, for a good part of the day.

And things have been piling up — bills, calls I meant to return, even ordinary housework. I feel embarrassed saying that, because I know I should be managing better. But yes… I suppose it has been low like that for stretches of at least a couple of weeks. Does that answer what you’re asking?

Would you say that you no longer care about doing the things you used to value, like your hobbies or responsibilities, not just because you’re overwhelmed, but because they don’t seem important or meaningful to you anymore?

I don’t think it’s that they don’t seem important anymore. No… I wouldn’t put it that way.

I still care about the things I’m supposed to care about, and the things I used to value. It’s more that I don’t always get to them, or I feel a bit stuck getting started. But I’d feel worse if they truly stopped mattering to me, and I don’t think that’s what’s happening.

Maybe I’m splitting hairs, but the meaning is still there. I’m just not always managing it very well. Is that a fair distinction?
Would you say that you’ve completely lost interest in all or almost all activities, including things you used to care about deeply?

No, I don’t think I’d say completely. That sounds too absolute.

There are things I still care about, even if I’m not doing them the way I used to, or I have to push myself more. It’s not like everything has gone blank or stopped mattering to me. I suppose I may not be as engaged as I was, but “completely lost interest in all or almost all activities”… no, I don’t think that would be accurate.

Does that make sense?

I suppose I may not be as engaged as I was, but “completely lost interest in all or almost all activities”… no, I don’t think that would be accurate.

Does that make sense?

Symptoms include persistent low mood most of the day, nearly every day, for more than two weeks; reduced interest or engagement in previously valued activities; tearfulness; irritability; and functional impairment in daily responsibilities. There is no evidence of psychotic features or complete loss of interest in all activities, ruling out more severe diagnoses.
